Such an object cannot be altered

facts.claim: and and or short-circuit and return the last operand evaluated, so '' or 'Trondheim' gives 'Trondheim'.

facts.claim: The tutorial's while-loop example prints the Fibonacci numbers below 10 as 0 1 1 2 3 5 8.

facts.claim: GeeksforGeeks lists three main types of machine learning (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement) and also covers semi-supervised and self-supervised learning.
GeeksforGeeks lists logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, KNN, naive Bayes and SVM as classification algorithms.
GeeksforGeeks lists K-Means, DBSCAN and mean-shift for clustering and PCA for dimensionality reduction.
GeeksforGeeks lists Q-learning and SARSA as reinforcement learning algorithms.
GeeksforGeeks gives BERT and GPT as examples of self-supervised models that predict masked words from context.
Jurafsky and Martin say handwritten classification rules can be fragile, and that the most common approach is supervised machine learning with a labeled training set and a learning algorithm.
Jurafsky and Martin call language-model pretraining self-supervised because the natural sequence of words supplies its own labels.

The 2007 Jurafsky and Martin draft lists decision trees, support vector machines, Gaussian mixture models and logistic regression as common classifiers, and stresses separate training and test sets and cross-validation.
scikit-learn's install page creates a virtual environment, activates it, and runs pip install -U scikit-learn (macOS and Linux use source sklearn-env/bin/activate).

NumPy is imported with import numpy as np.

NumPy arrays have ndim, shape and size attributes; a 3-by-4 array has shape (3, 4) and size 12.

In scikit-learn, estimators are fitted with fit(X, y) and used with predict; X has shape (n_samples, n_features).
Google's linear regression model is y' = b + w1x1, where y' is the predicted label, b the bias, w1 the weight and x1 the feature.
In Google's car example the learned bias is 34 and the weight is -4.6, so a 4,000-pound car is predicted at 15.6 miles per gallon.
Jurafsky and Martin (2007) use the word regression when the output is a real number and classification when it is one of a set of classes.

facts.claim: In the 2007 draft's made-up housing data the best-fit line is y = -4900x + 16550.

scikit-learn's LinearRegression fits its coefficients by minimizing the residual sum of squares.

check: Calculate the loss with the current weight and bias

facts.claim: In Google's worked example the loss (MSE) is 303.71 at iteration 1, and after six iterations it reaches 42.17.
check: Completing the process for six iterations

The 2007 draft chooses linear-regression weights to minimize the sum-squared error between predicted and observed values.
Google computes a probability by first calculating z = b + w1x1 + ... + wnxn and then passing z through the sigmoid, y' = 1 / (1 + e^-z).
In Google's sigmoid table z = -2 gives 0.119, z = 0 gives 0.50, z = 1 gives 0.731 and z = 2 gives 0.881.
At test time a logistic regression classifier computes the probability of each class and returns the higher-probability label.
check: we return the higher probability label

facts.claim: Jurafsky and Martin say logistic regression learns a weight for each feature plus a bias term, and passes the weighted sum z through the sigmoid, also called the logistic function.
The 2007 draft defines odds as the probability of being in a class divided by the probability of not being in it, and gives the example that probabilities .75 and .25 make odds of 3.
scikit-learn says logistic regression is implemented as a linear model for classification rather than regression, in terms of its nomenclature.
check: implemented as a linear model for classification rather than regression

Google says splitting the data into only a training set and a test set is not an optimal split, and recommends adding a validation set.
Google warns that the more often you reuse the same test set, the more likely the model fits that test set.

Google says overfitting means creating a model that matches (memorizes) the training set so closely that it fails to make correct predictions on new data, and lists an overly complex model as a cause.
check: matches (memorizes) the training set so closely that the model fails to make correct predictions on new data

facts.claim: scikit-learn calls evaluating a model on its own training data a methodological mistake, because a model that just repeats the labels it has seen would score perfectly yet predict nothing useful.
In k-fold cross-validation the training set is split into k parts, the model is trained on k-1 of them and validated on the last, and the reported score is the average over the k runs.
scikit-learn says preprocessing such as standardization should be learnt from a training set and applied to held-out data, and that a Pipeline can do this inside cross-validation.
check: similarly should be learnt from a training set and applied to held-out data for prediction

facts.claim: In scikit-learn's example a degree-1 polynomial underfits a noisy cosine, degree 4 fits well and degree 15 overfits, learning the noise of the training data.
The 2007 draft describes 10-fold cross-validation: repeat random training/test splits 10 times and average the error rates.
Jurafsky and Martin show that higher-order n-gram models copy their training text more closely, and a 4-gram model trained on Shakespeare reproduces a line from King John.
Google defines accuracy as (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN), recall as TP/(TP+FN) and precision as TP/(TP+FP).
Google says a model that always predicts negative on a dataset with 1% positives would score 99% accuracy yet be useless.
Jurafsky and Martin give a rare-class example: 100 tweets about pie among a million, where a classifier that says 'not about pie' every time reaches 99.99% accuracy and finds nothing.
Jurafsky and Martin define precision as true positives over true positives plus false positives, and recall as true positives over true positives plus false negatives.
In Jurafsky and Martin's three-class example, macroaveraged precision is .60 and microaveraged precision is .73, and microaveraging is dominated by the most frequent class.
In scikit-learn's confusion matrix, entry (i, j) counts observations actually in group i but predicted to be in group j, and for two classes ravel() gives tn, fp, fn, tp.
scikit-learn defines precision as tp/(tp+fp), recall as tp/(tp+fn), and the F-measure as their weighted harmonic mean, with F1 weighting them equally.
scikit-learn's example with y_true [0, 1, 0, 1] and y_pred [0, 1, 0, 0] shows precision 1.0, recall 0.5 and an F1 printed as 0.66..., which is the truncated form of 2/3 (0.667).
The 2007 draft says to compare a classifier with a most-frequent-class baseline and a human ceiling; human taggers agreed on about 96-97% of Penn Treebank tags.
The 2007 draft defines the F-measure as F1 = 2PR/(P+R), derived from a weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall.

scikit-learn describes nearest-neighbors classification as storing the training instances and assigning a query point the class with the most representatives among its k nearest neighbors, and says the best k is highly data-dependent.

most probable sense given that vector
naively assume that the features are independent of one another

highly dependent on the initialization of the centroids

scikit-learn describes clustering as working on unlabeled data.

check: cost and difficulty of producing reliably

facts.claim: The 2007 draft's Berkeley restaurant corpus has 9,332 sentences and a vocabulary of 1,446 words, and the bigram probability of 'i want english food' is about .000031.
